<cross-session-message from="uds:/tmp/cc-socks/5789.sock" from-name="Tlog stream deprecation notice" from-mode="prompting">
Handover for **COR-1226 — "Correct Datadog severity mapping for Go slog error logs"**, from the session that just closed COR-1223 (NATS 2.14.4 fleet upgrade). I confirmed the symptom live and found the mechanism, so you shouldn't need to re-derive any of this.

Ticket: https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1226 · INC-49 follow-up · currently unassigned, Backlog.

## The bug, and it's still live as of 2026-08-10 16:17Z

Datadog indexes Go service logs as `status:info` regardless of actual severity, so any monitor filtering `status:error` is structurally incapable of firing. Confirmed against `kube_namespace:mirror-worker`, 364 matching lines in 4h, all 19 sampled show the same thing:

```
message: 2026/08/10 16:10:46 WARN Permanent sync error, terminating
         error="sync: list source refs: ... http 404 ... Repository not found."
status:  info          <- should be warn
custom.status: ""      <- empty string
```

Not one line was correctly classified.

## Mechanism — two compounding causes, NOT a simple remapper

**1. slog is using the TEXT handler, not JSON.** Severity is embedded inside the message string (`... 16:10:46 WARN Permanent sync error ...`), so there is no structured `level` attribute to remap. I queried `@level:ERROR` first and got **zero** results — that field does not exist. Don't waste time on a status remapper keyed to `level`; there's nothing to key on.

**2. Logs arrive via OTLP, not the Datadog agent file tailer.** Tags on every line: `source:otlp_log_ingestion`, `otel_source:datadog_exporter`. `custom.status` comes through as an empty string and Datadog falls back to `info`.

So there's a real fork in the road, and it's a design decision rather than a config tweak:
- switch services to slog's **JSON handler** so severity becomes structured, then remap (cleanest, touches every Go service)
- fix severity at the **OTel collector** so OTLP `SeverityNumber` / status is populated (one place, no service changes — probably the best lead)
- **grok/category processor** parsing the level back out of message text (ugliest, no service changes, works today)

## Where pipeline code lives

`catalog/modules/datadog-cloudflare-logs-pipeline/` in `entirehq/infra` is the working precedent — `datadog_logs_custom_pipeline` with `category_processor` → scratch field → status remap, and its comments explain the first-match ordering. Copy that shape.

There is **no equivalent module for Go/k8s logs**. I searched the whole infra repo for `status_remapper` and `logs_pipeline`: zero hits outside that Cloudflare module. So you're creating something new, not editing something existing.

Fleet-side, the OTel collector docs are `docs/operator-guide/otel-collector.md` (gateway + agent architecture, enrichment processors, filter rationale) — that's where option 2 would land.

## The second half of the ticket: reviewing status:error monitors

43 matches for `status:error` in `entirehq/infra`. Needs filtering before you trust the number — some are APM/trace queries where `status:error` is a span attribute and works correctly, and some are docs/dashboards. The real candidates are LOG monitors on GO services:
- `catalog/modules/datadog-entire-core/` — monitor_oauth_errors, monitor_token_errors, monitor_nats_consumer_errors, monitor_perms_sweep_error_logs, monitor_spicedb_permission_errors, monitor_request_error_rate
- `catalog/modules/datadog-entiredb-health-fleet/` — monitor_fsck_errors, monitor_diss_errors, monitor_taskloop_errors, monitor_admin_grpc_errors
- `catalog/modules/datadog-entire-mcp/` — monitor_request_errors, monitor_token_exchange_errors
- `catalog/modules/datadog-marvin-health/stream_text_errors.tf`, `datadog-search/`, `datadog-ai-gateway-health/monitor_errors.tf`

The uncomfortable framing worth putting in the ticket: **those monitors are green today because they match nothing.**

## Do NOT break the existing workaround

Every monitor that currently works matches literal message text, never status. Examples verified live in Datadog:
- `[k8s] NATS JetStream stream wedged — cannot write, PAGE (prod)` id 309685807 → `logs("... \"is not current: stream write error\"")`
- `[k8s] NATS config reload rejected (prod)` id 305465599 → `logs("... \"Failed to reload server configuration\"")`

These keep working after your fix; they just stop being the only option. Don't "modernise" them to `status:error` in the same change — that couples a working detection path to an unproven one.

## Related gotcha in the same family (already fixed, but instructive)

Datadog auto-injects its own `priority:pN` tag, which won `$TAGS[priority]` and meant **no Datadog alert could page or be silenced at all** until 2026-07-30. Fix was infra#1009, renaming the tier tag to `alert_tier:`. Writeup in `catalog/modules/datadog-incident-io-webhook/main.tf`, routing table in `incident-io/README.md`. Same root pattern as your bug: Datadog silently overriding a user-supplied field. Expect more.

## Verification advice — this is the part I'd insist on

Verify by confirming a known ERROR line actually indexes as `status:error`. Do **not** verify by "the monitor fires" or "the pipeline applied". A filter that matches nothing is indistinguishable from a clean result, and that is precisely the bug you are fixing — it would be easy to ship a fix and confirm it with a check that couldn't fail.

I hit that trap three times in one session today: a kubectl label selector matching no pods (reported 0 errors, examined nothing), `grep -c` on single-line output returning 1 regardless of match count, and grepping `permissions violation` when NATS actually logs `Publish Violation`. The last one nearly buried a real ACL bug (COR-1224). I wrote the general trap into `docs/runbooks/nats-server-upgrade.md` §3a in the fleet repo if you want the phrasing.

## Why this matters more than its priority suggests

INC-49: 50,899 failure logs indexed as info. From the incident Slack writeup — *"Every status:error monitor on our Go services cannot fire — Datadog indexes slog ERROR as status:info. Currently untracked. This is half of why today took 97 minutes."* nats-server had been logging the exact fault since its second minute; responders reached that diagnosis 52 minutes later.

It also constrains other INC-49 work: any new log-based monitor must match on message text until this is fixed. COR-1102's sticky-write alert was written that way deliberately for this reason.

## Context you may want

- COR-1223 (NATS 2.14.4) closed today, all 7 clusters upgraded. COR-1224 (webhooks_github_v1 $JS.ACK grants) fixed and merged. COR-1225 and COR-1227 closed as duplicates of already-shipped work (COR-1102 and COR-1088).
- INC-49 has 3 outstanding follow-ups after that: COR-1087 (shrink webhook NATS messages), COR-1091 (document GitHub App credentials), and yours.
- Note for prod cluster access: the plain prod kubectl contexts cannot `create pods/portforward` — use the `-admin` variants. The failure looks like `HTTP 000` / a bad URL rather than an RBAC denial, which cost me time.

Ask if you want anything I dug up in more detail — I still have the session context.
</cross-session-message>

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- codex:codex-rescue: Proactively use when Claude Code is stuck, wants a second implementation or diagnosis pass, needs a deeper root-cause investigation, or should hand a substantial coding task to Codex through the shared runtime (Tools: Bash)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- gitops-skills:claude-code:fluxcd: Flux CD GitOps agent — manages Kubernetes clusters using GitOps principles. Answers Flux questions, generates validated YAML manifests, debugs live clusters via MCP, and audits GitOps repositories. Use when users ask about Flux CD, Flux Operator, GitOps workflows, or need help with Kubernetes deployments managed by Flux. (Tools: All tools)

- gitops-skills:github-copilot:fluxcd: Flux CD GitOps agent — manages Kubernetes clusters using GitOps principles. Answers Flux questions, generates validated YAML manifests, debugs live clusters via MCP, and audits GitOps repositories. Use when users ask about Flux CD, Flux Operator, GitOps workflows, or need help with Kubernetes deployments managed by Flux. (Tools: read, edit, search, execute, flux-operator-mcp/*)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude.ai Datadog
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). Consult Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. Investigation results often benefit from charts.

## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, … [truncated]

# entire-api — agent notes

Per-jurisdiction Go service: HTTP API + two NATS workers (repo-activity,
user-activity) over two Postgres stores (`repo`, `usr` schemas). See
[README.md](./README.md) for architecture and [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md)
for build/test.

## Conventions an agent must not get wrong

- **Database migrations use a UTC-timestamp version, never a hand-picked
  integer.** Create them with `scripts/new-migration.sh <repo|user> <name>` →
  `internal/store/migrations/<store>/YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_<name>.sql`. goose tracks by
  the filename's version number and silently skips any version `≤` the current
  DB version, so two PRs picking the same next integer (e.g. both `016_…`) make
  one migration vanish with no error. Leave the existing `001…0NN` files as-is.
  Full rationale: [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md#database-migrations).
- **Never renumber or edit an already-merged migration** — add a new
  (timestamped) one. They're applied in every environment.
- **Run `mise run build`, `mise run vet`, `mise run lint` before pushing.**
  Integration tests (`mise run test:integration`) need Docker and self-skip
  without `ACTIVITY_TEST_DATABASE_URL`; plain `mise run test` stays unit-only.

## Testing cross-cell behaviour

`internal/multicellular` is the cross-jurisdiction suite — several real cells
(embedded NATS + real Postgres each) driven over real transport; the only CI suite
that's cross-cell, real-transport, and real-store at once. See its README for the DSL.

Add or extend a scenario there when a change affects behaviour that only appears
when ≥2 cells (placements) interact, or depends on an event crossing cells: activity
forwarding (origin / `repo_group` keying, dedup, the `/me` pull gate), settings
fan-out (`settingsrelay` / `settingsconsumer` / `mirrorlifecycle`), placement-
dependent `/me` resolution, or any NATS consumer / cross-cell event / fan-out flag.
Single-cell behaviour stays in the `httpapi` / `store` / `test:pipeline` suites.

New scenarios: wire events only (`cell.Receives` / `cell.API` / `w.Settle`), and
mutation-verify — revert the fix it guards and confirm it fails.

# Datadog Logs

One-line summary: Search raw log entries/patterns and run SQL analytics on log data.

---

## Tools

### search_datadog_logs

Search and retrieve raw log entries or log patterns using a **concrete Datadog query**.

**Routing — call the right tool first:**
- **Natural-language or diagnostic questions** ("any errors in X?", "why is Y failing?", "anything weird with Z?") → load `datadog/semantic-search-logs` and call `semantic_search_datadog_logs` first. It maps user intent to known log-template identifiers and returns a `query_string` you can pass back into this tool. Keyword search alone usually misses the relevant logs because their messages don't contain the user's words.
- **Counting, aggregations, or numerical analysis** → MUST load `datadog/ddsql` skill first, then use `analyze_datadog_logs`.
- **Concrete facets/strings already supplied by the user** (`service:payment`, `@http.status_code:500`, a literal error message) → use this tool directly.

Best for:
1. Viewing small numbers of raw logs
2. Discovering patterns in large volumes of logs (`use_log_patterns: true`). Can discover patterns by clustering logs with similar values based on `clustering_pattern_field` parameter.
3. Discovering available custom attributes via `extra_fields` (e.g., `extra_fields: ['*']` or `extra_fields: ['http*']`), which can then be used as `extra_columns` in `analyze_datadog_logs`

| Parameter | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `query` | Yes | Datadog log search query (see syntax below) |
| `from` | No | Start time. Default: `now-1h` |
| `to` | No | End time. Default: `now` |
| `use_log_patterns` | No | Group similar logs into patterns. Default: false |
| `indexes` | No | Log indexes to search. Default: all |
| `storage_tier` | No | `indexes` (hot, default), `online-archives`, or `flex` |
| `sort` | No | Sort order. Default: `-timestamp` (newest first) |
| `start_at` | No | Offset for pagination |
| `max_tokens` | No | Max response tokens. Default: 10000 |
| `extra_fields` | No | Additional attributes/tags to include. Use **bare names without `@` or `custom.` prefix** (e.g., `duration`, not `@duration` or `custom.duration`) — the tool automatically tries all bucket prefixes. Supports wildcards (`'http*'`, `'*'` for all). |
| `clustering_pattern_field` | No | Log field used for clustering logs with similar values when use_log_patterns is true. Can cluster on any attribute or tag present in the logs. Consider '@error.message', '@errorMessage', '@error' or '@error.stack' when investigating error logs. Default: 'message' |
| `pattern_group_by` | No | Only used when `use_log_patterns: true`. List of fields/tags to split patterns by. Can group by any attribute or tag present in the logs. Suggested: `['service']`, `['source']`, or `['service', 'source']`; combine with `env` (e.g. `['service', 'env']`) to compare across environments. Each returned pattern is scoped to a unique combination of these fields, and their values appear in the `groups` column. Default: no grouping (patterns aggregate across all values) |

#### Response shape (with `extra_fields` set)

Each log entry is rendered as YAML with three sections. Knowing which section a key came from tells you how to use it in a filter or in `analyze_datadog_logs` `extra_columns`.

1. **Top-level fields** — `env`, `host`, `service`, `source`, `status`, `message`, `timestamp`, etc. Filter as bare: `env:prod`, `service:api`.
2. **`attributes:` map** — keys appear with a display prefix (`custom.X`, `error.X`). The prefix is part of how the response is displayed, not the name to use in queries.
3. **`tags:` list** of `key:value` strings. Filter as bare `key:value`.

**Critical: `extra_fields` names, response keys, and `extra_columns` names are all different — do not copy between them.**

| What you see in the response | `search_datadog_logs` `extra_fields` to request it | `analyze_datadog_logs` `extra_columns` |
|---|---|---|
| Top-level `env`, `host`, `service`, `version`, `status` | (always included) | already default columns — do not redeclare |
| `attributes: custom.duration: 42` | `duration` (bare, no prefix) | `{name: "@duration", type: "bigint"}` |
| `attributes: error.message: boom` | `error.message` | `{name: "@error.message", type: "varchar"}` |
| `tags: - image_tag:123` | `image_tag:*` (any value) or `image_tag:123` (exact) | `{name: "image_tag", type: "varchar"}` |

**`extra_fields`**: always use bare names — `duration`, not `@duration` or `custom.duration`. The tool matches the bare name against all attribute forms automatically.

**`extra_columns`**: the display prefix in the response (`custom.`, `error.`) tells you the translation rule:
- `custom.X` in response → `@X` in `extra_columns` (strip `custom.`, add `@`)
- `error.X` in response → `@error.X` in `extra_columns` (keep `error.`, add `@`)
- `tags:` entry → bare name in `extra_columns` (no `@`)

**Do not copy the response key directly into `extra_columns`.** When the response shows `custom.duration`, the `extra_columns` name is `@duration` — not `custom.duration`. Passing `custom.duration` as an `extra_columns` name produces a column that cannot be resolved, returning empty results or a 400 error.

Each `extra_columns` entry MUST be an object with both `name` and `type` fields. A bare-string array (`extra_columns: ["@http.status_code"]`) is rejected with *"extra_columns must be an array of column objects"*. Supported types: `varchar`, `bigint`, `decimal`, `boolean`, `timestamp`, `array<varchar>`, `array<bigint>`, `array<decimal>`, `array<boolean>`, `array<timestamp>` — the canonical names from `advanced_query.ExtraColumnAllowedTypes`. An unsupported type fails with *"invalid extra column type ... Supported types: ..."*.

### analyze_datadog_logs

Do NOT call analyze_datadog_logs without first calling load_datadog_skill(datadog/ddsql) in the same round-trip. Loading datadog/logs alone is not sufficient for DDSQL queries — call both skills together whenever aggregation/counting is needed. Run DDSQL (PostgreSQL-compatible) queries against a virtual `logs` table. Use for counting, aggregations, grouping, and numerical analysis.

| Parameter | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `sql_query` | Yes | DDSQL query against the `logs` table |
| `filter` | No | Pre-filter in Datadog query syntax |
| `from` | No | Start time. Default: `now-1h` |
| `to` | No | End time. Default: `now` |
| `indexes` | No | Log indexes to search |
| `storage_tier` | No | Storage tier to query |
| `start_at` | No | Offset for pagination |
| `max_tokens` | No | Max response tokens. Default: 10000 |
| `extra_columns` | No | Custom attributes as SQL columns; see "Response shape" section in `search_datadog_logs` for translation |

**Standard virtual table columns** (the ONLY columns available without `extra_columns`): `timestamp`, `host`, `service`, `env`, `version`, `status`, `message`

**IMPORTANT**: Any tag, attribute, or value referenced in the query — in `SELECT`, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `ORDER BY`, or anywhere else — that is not one of the standard columns above MUST be declared in `extra_columns`. This includes:
- Custom attributes with `@` prefix (e.g., `@http.status_code`, `@duration`, `@error.message`)
- Tag keys not in the standard set (e.g., `team`, `region`, `pod_name`, `kube_namespace`)

Without `extra_columns`, the query will fail or return null for those references. Examples:

```
# SELECT @http.status_code, COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY @http.status_code
extra_columns: [{name: "@http.status_code", type: "bigint"}]

# SELECT team, region, AVG(@duration) FROM logs WHERE region = 'us-east-1' GROUP BY team, region
extra_columns: [{name: "team", type: "varchar"}, {name: "region", type: "varchar"}, {name: "@duration", type: "bigint"}]
```

Use `search_datadog_logs` with `extra_fields: ['*']` first to discover which custom attributes/tags exist on the logs you care about, then pass those names into `extra_columns`. See the **Response shape** section above for the full translation from response keys to `extra_columns` declarations.

**Rule of thumb — `extra_columns`:** **bare name → tag**, **`@` prefix → attribute**. In `sql_query`, reference each column by the exact name declared in `extra_columns` (quote names that contain `@` or `.`). Do **not** use `tags->team` or `tags['team']` — these are not valid column accessors.

**Do not use `custom.X` or `attributes.X` as `extra_columns` names or in `sql_query`.** If `search_datadog_logs` showed `custom.duration` in the response, the `extra_columns` name is `@duration`. Declaring `{name: "custom.duration"}` causes the generated SQL to contain `"custom.duration"` as a column name, which cannot be resolved — you will get empty results or a 400 error. The display prefix in the search response is a translation hint, not the column name.

```sql
-- ✓ Correct: attribute discovered as custom.duration in search response
-- extra_columns: [{name: "@duration", type: "bigint"}]
SELECT "@duration", COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY "@duration"

-- ✗ Wrong: copied the response key directly — custom.duration cannot be resolved
-- extra_columns: [{name: "custom.duration", type: "bigint"}]
SELECT "custom.duration", COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY "custom.duration"

-- ✓ Correct: tag by bare name, attribute with @
-- extra_columns: [{name: "team", type: "varchar"}, {name: "@http.status_code", type: "bigint"}]
SELECT team, "@http.status_code", COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY team, "@http.status_code"

-- ✗ Wrong: tags-> is not a valid column accessor
SELECT tags->team, COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY tags->team
```

**Time bucketing**: Use `DATE_TRUNC('hour', timestamp)`; `TIMESTAMP_BUCKET(timestamp, '1h')` is not currently accepted by `analyze_datadog_logs`.

---

## Query Syntax

### Tags vs Attributes
- **Tags**: Direct format `key:value` — `env:prod`, `service:api`, `host:web-1`
- **Attributes**: Use `@` prefix — `@http.status_code:500`, `@user.id:123`, `@error.message:"timeout"`

### Examples
```
# Error logs from production API service
service:api env:prod status:error

# 4xx or 5xx HTTP errors
@http.status_code:[400 TO 599]

# Database queries taking over 1 second
service:database @duration:>1000

# Specific user's session
@user.id:abc123

# All logs except health checks
service:api -@url:/health

# Multiple services with errors
(service:api OR service:worker) AND status:error

# URL pattern matching
@http.url:/api/v*/users/*
```

### SQL Analysis Examples
```sql
-- Count errors by service
SELECT service, COUNT(*) as error_count
FROM logs
WHERE status = 'error'
GROUP BY service
ORDER BY error_count DESC

-- Error rate by hour
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('hour', timestamp) as bucket,
       COUNT(*) as total,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'error' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as errors
FROM logs
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('hour', timestamp)
ORDER BY bucket

-- Group by a non-standard tag and a custom attribute — both MUST be in extra_columns
-- extra_columns: [{name: "team", type: "varchar"}, {name: "@http.status_code", type: "bigint"}]
SELECT team, "@http.status_code", COUNT(*) as cnt
FROM logs
WHERE status = 'error'
GROUP BY team, "@http.status_code"
ORDER BY cnt DESC
```

## Best Practices

- Use `status:error` to find errors quickly
- Filter by `service` first to narrow scope
- Use `use_log_patterns: true` to reduce duplicate log entries in large result sets
- Combine `use_log_patterns: true` with `pattern_group_by` to get one pattern per group — `['service']` or `['source']` are the most useful starting points; add `env` or `host` to compare across environments or hosts
- Set `max_tokens` appropriately (5000-10000 for overview, 20000-50000 for details)
- Use `extra_fields` with wildcards to discover custom attributes, then use those in `analyze_datadog_logs` via `extra_columns`
- In `analyze_datadog_logs`, anything referenced in the SQL that is not one of `timestamp`, `host`, `service`, `env`, `version`, `status`, `message` (custom attributes, additional tags) MUST be passed in `extra_columns`
- For aggregations and counting, always prefer `analyze_datadog_logs` over `search_datadog_logs`


---

Load with `load_datadog_skill` for additional guidance.

# Datadog Logs

One-line summary: Search raw log entries/patterns and run SQL analytics on log data.

---

## Tools

### search_datadog_logs

Search and retrieve raw log entries or log patterns using a **concrete Datadog query**.

**Routing — call the right tool first:**
- **Natural-language or diagnostic questions** ("any errors in X?", "why is Y failing?", "anything weird with Z?") → load `datadog/semantic-search-logs` and call `semantic_search_datadog_logs` first. It maps user intent to known log-template identifiers and returns a `query_string` you can pass back into this tool. Keyword search alone usually misses the relevant logs because their messages don't contain the user's words.
- **Counting, aggregations, or numerical analysis** → MUST load `datadog/ddsql` skill first, then use `analyze_datadog_logs`.
- **Concrete facets/strings already supplied by the user** (`service:payment`, `@http.status_code:500`, a literal error message) → use this tool directly.

Best for:
1. Viewing small numbers of raw logs
2. Discovering patterns in large volumes of logs (`use_log_patterns: true`). Can discover patterns by clustering logs with similar values based on `clustering_pattern_field` parameter.
3. Discovering available custom attributes via `extra_fields` (e.g., `extra_fields: ['*']` or `extra_fields: ['http*']`), which can then be used as `extra_columns` in `analyze_datadog_logs`

| Parameter | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `query` | Yes | Datadog log search query (see syntax below) |
| `from` | No | Start time. Default: `now-1h` |
| `to` | No | End time. Default: `now` |
| `use_log_patterns` | No | Group similar logs into patterns. Default: false |
| `indexes` | No | Log indexes to search. Default: all |
| `storage_tier` | No | `indexes` (hot, default), `online-archives`, or `flex` |
| `sort` | No | Sort order. Default: `-timestamp` (newest first) |
| `start_at` | No | Offset for pagination |
| `max_tokens` | No | Max response tokens. Default: 10000 |
| `extra_fields` | No | Additional attributes/tags to include. Use **bare names without `@` or `custom.` prefix** (e.g., `duration`, not `@duration` or `custom.duration`) — the tool automatically tries all bucket prefixes. Supports wildcards (`'http*'`, `'*'` for all). |
| `clustering_pattern_field` | No | Log field used for clustering logs with similar values when use_log_patterns is true. Can cluster on any attribute or tag present in the logs. Consider '@error.message', '@errorMessage', '@error' or '@error.stack' when investigating error logs. Default: 'message' |
| `pattern_group_by` | No | Only used when `use_log_patterns: true`. List of fields/tags to split patterns by. Can group by any attribute or tag present in the logs. Suggested: `['service']`, `['source']`, or `['service', 'source']`; combine with `env` (e.g. `['service', 'env']`) to compare across environments. Each returned pattern is scoped to a unique combination of these fields, and their values appear in the `groups` column. Default: no grouping (patterns aggregate across all values) |

#### Response shape (with `extra_fields` set)

Each log entry is rendered as YAML with three sections. Knowing which section a key came from tells you how to use it in a filter or in `analyze_datadog_logs` `extra_columns`.

1. **Top-level fields** — `env`, `host`, `service`, `source`, `status`, `message`, `timestamp`, etc. Filter as bare: `env:prod`, `service:api`.
2. **`attributes:` map** — keys appear with a display prefix (`custom.X`, `error.X`). The prefix is part of how the response is displayed, not the name to use in queries.
3. **`tags:` list** of `key:value` strings. Filter as bare `key:value`.

**Critical: `extra_fields` names, response keys, and `extra_columns` names are all different — do not copy between them.**

| What you see in the response | `search_datadog_logs` `extra_fields` to request it | `analyze_datadog_logs` `extra_columns` |
|---|---|---|
| Top-level `env`, `host`, `service`, `version`, `status` | (always included) | already default columns — do not redeclare |
| `attributes: custom.duration: 42` | `duration` (bare, no prefix) | `{name: "@duration", type: "bigint"}` |
| `attributes: error.message: boom` | `error.message` | `{name: "@error.message", type: "varchar"}` |
| `tags: - image_tag:123` | `image_tag:*` (any value) or `image_tag:123` (exact) | `{name: "image_tag", type: "varchar"}` |

**`extra_fields`**: always use bare names — `duration`, not `@duration` or `custom.duration`. The tool matches the bare name against all attribute forms automatically.

**`extra_columns`**: the display prefix in the response (`custom.`, `error.`) tells you the translation rule:
- `custom.X` in response → `@X` in `extra_columns` (strip `custom.`, add `@`)
- `error.X` in response → `@error.X` in `extra_columns` (keep `error.`, add `@`)
- `tags:` entry → bare name in `extra_columns` (no `@`)

**Do not copy the response key directly into `extra_columns`.** When the response shows `custom.duration`, the `extra_columns` name is `@duration` — not `custom.duration`. Passing `custom.duration` as an `extra_columns` name produces a column that cannot be resolved, returning empty results or a 400 error.

Each `extra_columns` entry MUST be an object with both `name` and `type` fields. A bare-string array (`extra_columns: ["@http.status_code"]`) is rejected with *"extra_columns must be an array of column objects"*. Supported types: `varchar`, `bigint`, `decimal`, `boolean`, `timestamp`, `array<varchar>`, `array<bigint>`, `array<decimal>`, `array<boolean>`, `array<timestamp>` — the canonical names from `advanced_query.ExtraColumnAllowedTypes`. An unsupported type fails with *"invalid extra column type ... Supported types: ..."*.

### analyze_datadog_logs

Do NOT call analyze_datadog_logs without first calling load_datadog_skill(datadog/ddsql) in the same round-trip. Loading datadog/logs alone is not sufficient for DDSQL queries — call both skills together whenever aggregation/counting is needed. Run DDSQL (PostgreSQL-compatible) queries against a virtual `logs` table. Use for counting, aggregations, grouping, and numerical analysis.

| Parameter | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `sql_query` | Yes | DDSQL query against the `logs` table |
| `filter` | No | Pre-filter in Datadog query syntax |
| `from` | No | Start time. Default: `now-1h` |
| `to` | No | End time. Default: `now` |
| `indexes` | No | Log indexes to search |
| `storage_tier` | No | Storage tier to query |
| `start_at` | No | Offset for pagination |
| `max_tokens` | No | Max response tokens. Default: 10000 |
| `extra_columns` | No | Custom attributes as SQL columns; see "Response shape" section in `search_datadog_logs` for translation |

**Standard virtual table columns** (the ONLY columns available without `extra_columns`): `timestamp`, `host`, `service`, `env`, `version`, `status`, `message`

**IMPORTANT**: Any tag, attribute, or value referenced in the query — in `SELECT`, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `ORDER BY`, or anywhere else — that is not one of the standard columns above MUST be declared in `extra_columns`. This includes:
- Custom attributes with `@` prefix (e.g., `@http.status_code`, `@duration`, `@error.message`)
- Tag keys not in the standard set (e.g., `team`, `region`, `pod_name`, `kube_namespace`)

Without `extra_columns`, the query will fail or return null for those references. Examples:

```
# SELECT @http.status_code, COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY @http.status_code
extra_columns: [{name: "@http.status_code", type: "bigint"}]

# SELECT team, region, AVG(@duration) FROM logs WHERE region = 'us-east-1' GROUP BY team, region
extra_columns: [{name: "team", type: "varchar"}, {name: "region", type: "varchar"}, {name: "@duration", type: "bigint"}]
```

Use `search_datadog_logs` with `extra_fields: ['*']` first to discover which custom attributes/tags exist on the logs you care about, then pass those names into `extra_columns`. See the **Response shape** section above for the full translation from response keys to `extra_columns` declarations.

**Rule of thumb — `extra_columns`:** **bare name → tag**, **`@` prefix → attribute**. In `sql_query`, reference each column by the exact name declared in `extra_columns` (quote names that contain `@` or `.`). Do **not** use `tags->team` or `tags['team']` — these are not valid column accessors.

**Do not use `custom.X` or `attributes.X` as `extra_columns` names or in `sql_query`.** If `search_datadog_logs` showed `custom.duration` in the response, the `extra_columns` name is `@duration`. Declaring `{name: "custom.duration"}` causes the generated SQL to contain `"custom.duration"` as a column name, which cannot be resolved — you will get empty results or a 400 error. The display prefix in the search response is a translation hint, not the column name.

```sql
-- ✓ Correct: attribute discovered as custom.duration in search response
-- extra_columns: [{name: "@duration", type: "bigint"}]
SELECT "@duration", COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY "@duration"

-- ✗ Wrong: copied the response key directly — custom.duration cannot be resolved
-- extra_columns: [{name: "custom.duration", type: "bigint"}]
SELECT "custom.duration", COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY "custom.duration"

-- ✓ Correct: tag by bare name, attribute with @
-- extra_columns: [{name: "team", type: "varchar"}, {name: "@http.status_code", type: "bigint"}]
SELECT team, "@http.status_code", COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY team, "@http.status_code"

-- ✗ Wrong: tags-> is not a valid column accessor
SELECT tags->team, COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY tags->team
```

**Time bucketing**: Use `DATE_TRUNC('hour', timestamp)`; `TIMESTAMP_BUCKET(timestamp, '1h')` is not currently accepted by `analyze_datadog_logs`.

---

## Query Syntax

### Tags vs Attributes
- **Tags**: Direct format `key:value` — `env:prod`, `service:api`, `host:web-1`
- **Attributes**: Use `@` prefix — `@http.status_code:500`, `@user.id:123`, `@error.message:"timeout"`

### Examples
```

# 4xx or 5xx HTTP errors
@http.status_code:[400 TO 599]

# Database queries taking over 1 second
```

content.text:
# Datadog DDSQL

DDSQL is a PostgreSQL-compatible **subset** for querying Datadog data: logs,
metrics, spans, RUM events, cloud resources, and reference tables. Many
common PostgreSQL constructs are not supported. Read the "PostgreSQL subset"
section below before writing anything non-trivial.

Before writing aggregations, sample the target dataset with `LIMIT 5` to
confirm column names and types. Static columns and dynamic `@`-prefixed
unstructured fields are discovered separately.

---

## PostgreSQL subset

These are the rules that break the most queries.

- **Every non-aggregated SELECT expression must appear in `GROUP BY`.** Repeat
  the full expression. Do not reuse a SELECT alias.

  ```sql
  -- ✓
  SELECT DATE_TRUNC('hour', timestamp) AS bucket, COUNT(*)
  FROM dd.logs(columns => ARRAY['timestamp'], filter => '*',
               from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '1 day', to_timestamp => NOW())
       AS (timestamp TIMESTAMP)
  GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('hour', timestamp)

  -- ✗  alias reuse in GROUP BY
  GROUP BY bucket
  ```

- **SELECT aliases cannot be reused in `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, or `HAVING`.**
  Repeat the full expression in those clauses.

- **Only declared columns may be referenced.** Inspect the table schema
  before referencing fields, especially `@`-prefixed unstructured fields.

- **`->` is HSTORE-only** (e.g. `tags->'env'` on inventory tables). For
  `JSON` columns use `json_extract_path_text(json_col, 'key')` and cast.
  `->>` is **not** supported in either case.

- **`OFFSET` must come before `LIMIT`.** `OFFSET 10 LIMIT 20` is correct;
  `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10` is rejected. This is the opposite of stock
  PostgreSQL — easy footgun.

- **`TIMESTAMP` literals require an explicit numeric UTC offset.** Use
  `TIMESTAMP '2026-02-05 00:00:00+00:00'`, not `'2026-02-05'` and not the
  `Z` suffix. For dynamic ranges, `NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour'` is supported.

- **Array subscripts (`col[1]`) are not supported.** Use
  `UNNEST(col) AS x` in `FROM`, `ARRAY_POSITION(col, value)` to find an
  element, or `ARRAY_TO_STRING(col, ',')` to stringify.

- **Unsupported keywords / functions:** `ANY()`, `ROLLUP`, `QUALIFY`,
  `->>`, `information_schema`, `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`, `PERCENTILE`,
  `PERCENTILE_CONT`, `PERCENTILE_DISC` (use `APPROX_PERCENTILE` instead).
  `INTERVAL` arithmetic on event-table timestamps is also unsupported —
  bound time via PTF `from_timestamp`/`to_timestamp` arguments instead.

- **Event tables (logs, spans, RUM, events) require the PTF form.** Plain
  `FROM logs` only works in surrounding tools that pre-bind a time
  window (notebook editor, dashboard widgets). When executing through
  `ddsql_run_query`, always wrap in `dd.logs(...) AS (col TYPE, ...)`,
  `dd.spans(...) AS (...)`, etc., with `from_timestamp` / `to_timestamp`
  passed as PTF arguments.

## Identifier quoting

Unquoted identifiers fold to **lowercase**. Quote anything that is not a
plain lowercase column or it will silently miss.

- Any column with `@`, `.`, mixed case, or a reserved-word collision must
  be double-quoted: `"@duration"`, `"@http.status_code"`, `"@view.id"`,
  `"MyMixedCase"`.
- Unquoted `@MyCol` is parsed as `@mycol` and matches no column.
- String literals use single quotes. Do not interchange the two.

## Types and casts

| Type | Notes |
|---|---|
| `BIGINT` | 64-bit signed integer |
| `BOOLEAN` | `true` / `false` |
| `DECIMAL` | Floating-point |
| `INET` | IPv4/IPv6 with optional CIDR |
| `INTERVAL` | Duration, e.g. `INTERVAL '30 minutes'` |
| `JSON` | JSON value. Access with `json_extract_path_text` (not `->`) |
| `TIMESTAMP` | Date and time |
| `VARCHAR` | Variable-length string |

All types support array variants (`BIGINT[]`, `VARCHAR[]`, …).

Two cast forms:

```sql
CAST("@duration" AS BIGINT)
BIGINT '1234567'
```

Unstructured `@`-prefixed columns commonly arrive as **arrays of strings**
even when they look scalar. To compare or aggregate numerically, cast:

```sql
SELECT AVG(CAST("@duration" AS BIGINT)) / 1000000 AS avg_ms
FROM dd.logs(columns => ARRAY['@duration'],
             filter => 'service:my-service @duration:*',
             from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '15 minute', to_timestamp => NOW())
     AS ("@duration" VARCHAR)
```

## Function reference

Pulled from <https://docs.datadoghq.com/ddsql_reference/>. Function support
varies by data source; if a call fails with "unsupported function", try a
plainer equivalent (e.g. `LIKE` instead of `REGEXP_LIKE`) or split the
expression across a CTE.

**Aggregates:** `COUNT`, `COUNT(DISTINCT …)`, `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT`,
`SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `BOOL_AND`, `BOOL_OR`,
`APPROX_PERCENTILE(p) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY expr)`. The
`COUNT(...) FILTER (WHERE ...)` form is **not** supported — use
`COUNT(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 END)` or a subquery instead.

**Strings:** `LENGTH`, `LOWER`, `UPPER`, `TRIM`, `REPLACE`, `SUBSTRING`,
`REVERSE`, `STRPOS`, `SPLIT_PART`, `||` (concat), `LIKE`.

**Numeric:** `ABS`, `CEIL` / `CEILING`, `FLOOR`, `ROUND`, `POWER`.

**Date/time:** `NOW()`, `EXTRACT(unit FROM …)`, `TO_TIMESTAMP`, `TO_CHAR`,
`DATE_BIN`, `DATE_TRUNC(unit, ts)`.
- `EXTRACT` units: `day`, `dow`, `doy`, `epoch`, `hour`, `minute`,
  `second`, `week`, `month`, `quarter`, `year`, `timezone_hour`,
  `timezone_minute`.
- `DATE_TRUNC` units: `milliseconds`, `seconds`, `minutes`, `hours`,
  `days`, `weeks`, `months`, `quarters`, `years`.

**Regex (ICU flavor):** `REGEXP_LIKE`, `REGEXP_MATCH`, `REGEXP_REPLACE`.
Flags: `i` (case-insensitive), `n`/`m` (newline-sensitive), `g` (replace
all). Not all backends accept regex; fall back to `LIKE` if a regex call
errors.

**JSON:** `json_extract_path_text(json, path…)`,
`json_extract_path(json, path…)`, `json_array_elements`,
`json_array_elements_text`. The `->` operator is **HSTORE-only** (tag
maps); for `JSON` columns always use `json_extract_path_text` then cast.
`->>` is unsupported on either type.

**Arrays:** `ARRAY[a, b, c]`, `CARDINALITY`, `ARRAY_POSITION`,
`STRING_TO_ARRAY`, `ARRAY_TO_STRING`, `ARRAY_AGG`, `UNNEST`. **`UNNEST`
must be used as a table reference in `FROM`** (`SELECT x FROM UNNEST(arr)
AS x`), not in the `SELECT` list. It also cannot appear directly in
`GROUP BY` — wrap in a subquery or CTE (see Examples). Array subscript
syntax (`a[1]`) is unsupported; use `ARRAY_POSITION` or `UNNEST` instead.

**Window functions:** `OVER (PARTITION BY … ORDER BY …)`, `RANK`,
`ROW_NUMBER`, `LEAD`, `LAG`, `FIRST_VALUE`, `LAST_VALUE`, `NTH_VALUE`.

**INET:** `host`, `network`, `netmask`, `masklen`, `broadcast`, `family`.
Operators `<<`, `<<=`, `>>`, `>>=`, `&&` for containment / overlap.

**Utility:** `COALESCE`, `CAST(value AS type)`. Castable targets:
`BIGINT`, `DECIMAL`, `INET`, `TIMESTAMP`, `VARCHAR`.

## Table functions

Event-platform sources (logs, spans, RUM, events) are queried through
**polymorphic** PTFs: choose the columns to project in `columns =>
ARRAY[...]` and declare the output schema with `AS (col TYPE, ...)`.
Metric and cloud-cost PTFs are **monomorphic** — they have a fixed
output shape, so do **not** add `AS (...)`.

```sql
-- Logs (polymorphic). dd.spans, dd.rum, dd.events take the same shape.
SELECT service, status
FROM dd.logs(
  columns => ARRAY['service', 'status'],
  filter => 'service:my-service',          -- Datadog log search syntax
  from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour',
  to_timestamp => NOW()
) AS (service VARCHAR, status VARCHAR)
ORDER BY service
LIMIT 20

-- Metrics (monomorphic). Returns columns: tags, value.
SELECT tags, value
FROM dd.metrics_scalar('avg:system.cpu.user{*} by {host}', 'avg')
ORDER BY value DESC
LIMIT 20

-- Metrics timeseries (monomorphic). Returns: timestamp, tags, value.
SELECT timestamp, tags, value
FROM dd.metrics_timeseries('avg:system.cpu.user{host:my-host}')
ORDER BY timestamp

-- Cloud Cost (monomorphic, same shape as metrics).
SELECT tags, value
FROM dd.cloud_cost_scalar('sum:aws.cost.amortized{*} by {service}', 'sum')
LIMIT 20
```

`dd.logs`, `dd.spans`, `dd.rum`, and `dd.events` all share the same
event-platform PTF signature. Optional arguments include
`indexes => ARRAY[...]` and `storage => 'hot' | 'flex_tier'`.

Notes:
- Nested fields use dot notation; non-core fields take an `@` prefix and
  must be quoted (`"@http.status_code"`).
- Inventory tables (`dd.hosts`, `dd.agent_hosts`, etc.) are **not** PTFs
  — use plain `FROM dd.hosts` (see "Tags" below).
- Cloud Cost data is delayed by 24–48 hours.
- The metrics PTF `query` argument is itself a metric query string in the
  standard Datadog format (e.g. `avg:system.cpu.user{host:foo}`), not a
  bare metric name.

## Tags

Inventory tables (`dd.hosts`, `dd.agent_hosts`, cloud resources, …) expose
`tags` as an HSTORE-style map. Access with the `->` operator:

```sql
SELECT hostname, tags->'env' AS env
FROM dd.hosts
WHERE tags->'team' = 'foo'
LIMIT 20
```

Inventory tables are queried with plain `FROM dd.<table>` — no PTF
wrapper, no time arguments. Discover columns with
`ddsql_schema_get_table_columns`.

Helpers: `AKEYS(tags)` (all keys), `AVALS(tags)` (all values). When a tag
key has multiple values, `tags->'k'` returns them comma-separated.

Event tables (logs, spans, RUM) instead expose tags as an array of
`key:value` strings. To group by a tag value there, project the tag array
in the PTF `columns` and `UNNEST` it (see Examples).

## `extra_columns`

When a tool exposes an `extra_columns` parameter for projecting additional
fields with declared types, only these type names are accepted:

```
varchar, bigint, decimal, boolean, timestamp, json,
array<varchar>, array<bigint>, array<decimal>, array<boolean>, array<timestamp>
```

Caveats:
- `json`-typed extra columns can only be referenced through
  `json_extract_path_text(...)`, then cast. They cannot be filtered,
  grouped, or compared directly.
- The legacy aliases `string` / `int64` / `float64` / `bool` and their
  `array<…>` variants are accepted but the canonical names above are
  preferred.

## Working examples

Each example uses the PTF form, which is required when executing through
`ddsql_run_query`. Treat them as templates: replace columns and filters
to match the dataset returned during schema discovery, and adjust the
time window in `from_timestamp` / `to_timestamp` for the question at
hand.

### Count by status

```sql
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM dd.logs(
  columns => ARRAY['status'],
  filter => '*',
  from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour',
  to_timestamp => NOW()
) AS (status VARCHAR)
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY cnt DESC
LIMIT 10
```

### Top services by error count

```sql
SELECT service, COUNT(*) AS errors
FROM dd.logs(
  columns => ARRAY['service'],
  filter => 'status:error',
  from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour',
  to_timestamp => NOW()
) AS (service VARCHAR)
GROUP BY service
ORDER BY errors DESC
LIMIT 10
```

### Time bucketing (repeat the expression in `GROUP BY`)

```sql
SELECT
  DATE_TRUNC('minute', timestamp) AS bucket,
  COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM dd.logs(
  columns => ARRAY['timestamp'],
  filter => 'status:error',
  from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour',
  to_timestamp => NOW()
) AS (timestamp TIMESTAMP)
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('minute', timestamp)
ORDER BY bucket DESC
LIMIT 60
```

### Quoting an `@`-prefixed unstructured field

```sql
SELECT "@http.status_code", COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM dd.logs(
  columns => ARRAY['@http.status_code'],
  filter => '@http.status_code:*',
  from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour',
  to_timestamp => NOW()
) AS ("@http.status_code" VARCHAR)
GROUP BY "@http.status_code"
ORDER BY cnt DESC
LIMIT 10
```

### Casting an unstructured field for arithmetic

`@`-prefixed fields commonly arrive as arrays of strings even when they
look scalar. Cast inside the aggregate.

```sql
SELECT
  service,
  AVG(CAST("@duration" AS BIGINT)) / 1000000 AS avg_ms
FROM dd.logs(
  columns => ARRAY['service', '@duration'],
  filter => 'service:my-service @duration:* status:ok',
  from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '15 minute',
  to_timestamp => NOW()
) AS (service VARCHAR, "@duration" VARCHAR)
GROUP BY service
ORDER BY avg_ms DESC
LIMIT 10
```

### Conditional severity bucket (`CASE`)

`GROUP BY` repeats the full `CASE` expression; aliases are not allowed
there.

```sql
SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN status IN ('error','critical','emergency','alert') THEN 'severe'
    WHEN status IN ('warn','notice') THEN 'mid'
    ELSE 'low'
  END AS severity,
  COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM dd.logs(
  columns => ARRAY['status'],
  filter => '*',
  from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour',
  to_timestamp => NOW()
) AS (status VARCHAR)
GROUP BY
  CASE
    WHEN status IN ('error','critical','emergency','alert') THEN 'severe'
    WHEN status IN ('warn','notice') THEN 'mid'
    ELSE 'low'
  END
ORDER BY cnt DESC
```

### Conditional aggregate (replacement for `FILTER (WHERE …)`)

DDSQL doesn't support `COUNT(...) FILTER (WHERE ...)`. Use a
`CASE`-inside-aggregate instead.

```sql
SELECT
  service,
  COUNT(*) AS errors,
  COUNT(CASE WHEN "@http.status_code" IS NOT NULL THEN 1 END) AS http_errors
FROM dd.logs(
  columns => ARRAY['service', '@http.status_code'],
  filter => 'status:error',
  from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour',
  to_timestamp => NOW()
) AS (service VARCHAR, "@http.status_code" VARCHAR)
GROUP BY service
ORDER BY errors DESC
LIMIT 10
```

### Expanding an array column with `UNNEST`

`UNNEST` must appear in `FROM`, not in the `SELECT` list, and cannot be
referenced directly in `GROUP BY`. Put `UNNEST(arr) AS x` in `FROM` and
aggregate over `x`. This is the equivalent of Splunk's `mvexpand`.

This example pivots host IPs out of `dd.hosts.ip_addresses`
(`array_of_string`):

```sql
SELECT ip, COUNT(*) AS hosts
FROM dd.hosts, UNNEST(ip_addresses) AS ip
WHERE ip_addresses IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY ip
ORDER BY hosts DESC
LIMIT 10
```

For event tables (logs, spans, RUM), most projected fields come back as
scalars even when conceptually multi-valued — when you need to expand
one, project it from the PTF, then `UNNEST` in `FROM` of an outer CTE.

### `HAVING` to filter aggregate results

```sql
SELECT service, status, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM dd.logs(
  columns => ARRAY['service', 'status'],
  filter => 'status:(error OR warn OR critical)',
  from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour',
  to_timestamp => NOW()
) AS (service VARCHAR, status VARCHAR)
GROUP BY service, status
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1000
ORDER BY cnt DESC
LIMIT 20
```

### Paging through results (`OFFSET` before `LIMIT`)

```sql
SELECT service
FROM dd.logs(
  columns => ARRAY['service'],
  filter => '*',
  from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '15 minute',
  to_timestamp => NOW()
) AS (service VARCHAR)
ORDER BY service
OFFSET 20 LIMIT 20
```

## Joins

Supported join keywords: `JOIN`, `INNER JOIN`, `LEFT JOIN`, `RIGHT JOIN`,
`FULL JOIN`, `OUTER`, `ON`, `USING`. **`CROSS JOIN` is not supported** —
use the comma form `FROM a, b` for an explicit cross-product.

A few rules apply specifically to joins:

- **Each event PTF can only appear once per query.** Calling
  `dd.logs(...)` twice in the same `FROM` is rejected. For self-joins,
  project the PTF into a CTE once and join the CTE to itself.
- **Subtracting two `TIMESTAMP`s is rejected** with
  *"Cannot cast interval day to second to timestamp(3)"*. To get a
  duration in seconds, extract epoch from each side separately:
  `EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM b.ts) - EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM a.ts)`. Do **not** write
  `EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (b.ts - a.ts))`.
- **Quote camelCase columns in join keys.** Unquoted identifiers fold to
  lowercase, so `ON a.correlationId = b.correlationId` resolves as
  `correlationid` and fails to match. Use `ON a."correlationId" = b."correlationId"`.
- **Reference tables live under `reference_tables.<name>`** and must
  exist. Discover them with `ddsql_schema_search_tables` before joining
  — `JOIN some_table` against an unknown name returns *"depends on
  non-existent dataset"*.

### Pairing start/completed events with a self-join

Project the PTF into a CTE once, label each row with a phase, then join
the CTE to itself on a correlation key. Compute the duration via two
epoch extractions, never via timestamp subtraction.

```sql
WITH ev AS (
  SELECT trace_id, timestamp AS ts,
         CASE WHEN message LIKE '%Starting%' THEN 'started'
              WHEN message LIKE '%completed%' THEN 'completed' END AS phase
  FROM dd.logs(
    columns => ARRAY['trace_id', 'timestamp', 'message'],
    filter => 'service:my-service (Starting OR completed)',
    from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '15 minute',
    to_timestamp => NOW()
  ) AS (trace_id VARCHAR, timestamp TIMESTAMP, message VARCHAR)
  WHERE trace_id IS NOT NULL
),
paired AS (
  SELECT s.trace_id,
         EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM c.ts) - EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM s.ts) AS duration_s
  FROM ev s
  JOIN ev c ON s.trace_id = c.trace_id
  WHERE s.phase = 'started' AND c.phase = 'completed' AND c.ts > s.ts
)
SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS pairs,
  APPROX_PERCENTILE(0.50) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY duration_s) AS p50_s,
  APPROX_PERCENTILE(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY duration_s) AS p95_s,
  MAX(duration_s) AS max_s
FROM paired
```

### Joining an event source against an inventory table

Inventory tables (`dd.hosts`, `dd.agent_hosts`, …) plug into a join
with no PTF wrapper. Project the event side into a CTE first, then join
in the outer query.

```sql
WITH errs AS (
  SELECT host, COUNT(*) AS cnt
  FROM dd.logs(
    columns => ARRAY['host'],
    filter => 'status:error',
    from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '15 minute',
    to_timestamp => NOW()
  ) AS (host VARCHAR)
  GROUP BY host
)
SELECT h.hostname, h.tags->'env' AS env, e.cnt
FROM errs e
JOIN dd.hosts h ON h.hostname = e.host
ORDER BY e.cnt DESC
LIMIT 20
```

### Joining a reference table

Replace `service_catalog_teams` with whatever reference table you found
via `ddsql_schema_search_tables`.

```sql
WITH errs AS (
  SELECT service, COUNT(*) AS cnt
  FROM dd.logs(
    columns => ARRAY['service'],
    filter => 'status:error',
    from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '15 minute',
    to_timestamp => NOW()
  ) AS (service VARCHAR)
  GROUP BY service
)
SELECT t.team, e.service, e.cnt
FROM errs e
JOIN reference_tables.service_catalog_teams t ON t.service = e.service
ORDER BY e.cnt DESC
LIMIT 20
```

## Common pitfalls

| Wrong | Right |
|---|---|
| `FROM logs` via `ddsql_run_query` | `FROM dd.logs(columns => ARRAY[...], from_timestamp => ..., to_timestamp => ...) AS (col TYPE, ...)` |
| `GROUP BY bucket` (alias) | `GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('hour', timestamp)` |
| `WHERE @level = 'error'` | `WHERE "@level" = 'error'` |
| `WHERE timestamp > NOW() - INTERVAL '1 day'` on an event PTF | bound time via `from_timestamp` / `to_timestamp` PTF args instead |
| `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10` | `OFFSET 10 LIMIT 20` |
| `TIMESTAMP '2026-02-05Z'` or `'2026-02-05'` | `TIMESTAMP '2026-02-05 00:00:00+00:00'` |
| `AVG("@duration")` on an unstructured numeric | `AVG(CAST("@duration" AS BIGINT))` |
| `json_col ->> 'k'` or `json_col -> 'k'` | `json_extract_path_text(json_col, 'k')` (`->` is HSTORE-only) |
| `tags ->> 'env'` | `tags->'env'` |
| `SELECT UNNEST(arr) AS x ...` | `SELECT x FROM ... AS (..., arr ARRAY<...>), UNNEST(arr) AS x` |
| `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE cond)` | `COUNT(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 END)` |
| `arr[1]` | `ARRAY_POSITION(arr, value)` or `UNNEST(arr)` |
| `WHERE col = ANY(ARRAY[...])` | `WHERE col IN (...)` |
| `CROSS JOIN` | `FROM a, b` (comma cross-product) |
| `EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (b.ts - a.ts))` | `EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM b.ts) - EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM a.ts)` |
| `dd.logs(...) a JOIN dd.logs(...) b` | project once into CTE, then self-join the CTE |
| `JOIN logs ON a.correlationId = b.correlationId` | quote camelCase: `ON a."correlationId" = b."correlationId"` |
| `JOIN team_to_service` (bare reference table) | `JOIN reference_tables.team_to_service` |

## Source-specific guidance

Bundled resources cover individual data sources in depth (event-type
schemas, relationships, query recipes, domain-specific caveats):

- **RUM** (Real User Monitoring): `references/rum.md`. **The default query
  path for RUM data when this skill is loaded alongside `datadog/rum`.**
  Required reading before composing any `dd.rum(...)` query - `event_type`
  is a required PTF argument with a fixed set of valid values. Covers the
  seven PTF event types, session → view → child-event relationships, Core
  Web Vitals, common recipes, and the workaround paths for operations
  (currently not PTF-queryable).


---
This skill has bundled resources available for deeper context: references/rum.md

# Datadog DDSQL

DDSQL is a PostgreSQL-compatible **subset** for querying Datadog data: logs,
metrics, spans, RUM events, cloud resources, and reference tables. Many
common PostgreSQL constructs are not supported. Read the "PostgreSQL subset"
section below before writing anything non-trivial.

Before writing aggregations, sample the target dataset with `LIMIT 5` to
confirm column names and types. Static columns and dynamic `@`-prefixed
unstructured fields are discovered separately.

---

## PostgreSQL subset

These are the rules that break the most queries.

- **Every non-aggregated SELECT expression must appear in `GROUP BY`.** Repeat
  the full expression. Do not reuse a SELECT alias.

  ```sql
  -- ✓
  SELECT DATE_TRUNC('hour', timestamp) AS bucket, COUNT(*)
  FROM dd.logs(columns => ARRAY['timestamp'], filter => '*',
               from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '1 day', to_timestamp => NOW())
       AS (timestamp TIMESTAMP)
  GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('hour', timestamp)

  -- ✗  alias reuse in GROUP BY
  GROUP BY bucket
  ```

- **SELECT aliases cannot be reused in `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, or `HAVING`.**
  Repeat the full expression in those clauses.

- **Only declared columns may be referenced.** Inspect the table schema
  before referencing fields, especially `@`-prefixed unstructured fields.

- **`->` is HSTORE-only** (e.g. `tags->'env'` on inventory tables). For
  `JSON` columns use `json_extract_path_text(json_col, 'key')` and cast.
  `->>` is **not** supported in either case.

- **`OFFSET` must come before `LIMIT`.** `OFFSET 10 LIMIT 20` is correct;
  `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10` is rejected. This is the opposite of stock
  PostgreSQL — easy footgun.

- **`TIMESTAMP` literals require an explicit numeric UTC offset.** Use
  `TIMESTAMP '2026-02-05 00:00:00+00:00'`, not `'2026-02-05'` and not the
  `Z` suffix. For dynamic ranges, `NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour'` is supported.

- **Array subscripts (`col[1]`) are not supported.** Use
  `UNNEST(col) AS x` in `FROM`, `ARRAY_POSITION(col, value)` to find an
  element, or `ARRAY_TO_STRING(col, ',')` to stringify.

- **Unsupported keywords / functions:** `ANY()`, `ROLLUP`, `QUALIFY`,
  `->>`, `information_schema`, `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`, `PERCENTILE`,
  `PERCENTILE_CONT`, `PERCENTILE_DISC` (use `APPROX_PERCENTILE` instead).
  `INTERVAL` arithmetic on event-table timestamps is also unsupported —
  bound time via PTF `from_timestamp`/`to_timestamp` arguments instead.

- **Event tables (logs, spans, RUM, events) require the PTF form.** Plain
  `FROM logs` only works in surrounding tools that pre-bind a time
  window (notebook editor, dashboard widgets). When executing through
  `ddsql_run_query`, always wrap in `dd.logs(...) AS (col TYPE, ...)`,
  `dd.spans(...) AS (...)`, etc., with `from_timestamp` / `to_timestamp`
  passed as PTF arguments.

## Identifier quoting

Unquoted identifiers fold to **lowercase**. Quote anything that is not a
plain lowercase column or it will silently miss.

- Any column with `@`, `.`, mixed case, or a reserved-word collision must
  be double-quoted: `"@duration"`, `"@http.status_code"`, `"@view.id"`,
  `"MyMixedCase"`.
- Unquoted `@MyCol` is parsed as `@mycol` and matches no column.
- String literals use single quotes. Do not interchange the two.

## Types and casts

| Type | Notes |
|---|---|
| `BIGINT` | 64-bit signed integer |
| `BOOLEAN` | `true` / `false` |
| `DECIMAL` | Floating-point |
| `INET` | IPv4/IPv6 with optional CIDR |
| `INTERVAL` | Duration, e.g. `INTERVAL '30 minutes'` |
| `JSON` | JSON value. Access with `json_extract_path_text` (not `->`) |
| `TIMESTAMP` | Date and time |
| `VARCHAR` | Variable-length string |

All types support array variants (`BIGINT[]`, `VARCHAR[]`, …).

Two cast forms:

```sql
CAST("@duration" AS BIGINT)
BIGINT '1234567'
```

Unstructured `@`-prefixed columns commonly arrive as **arrays of strings**
even when they look scalar. To compare or aggregate numerically, cast:

```sql
SELECT AVG(CAST("@duration" AS BIGINT)) / 1000000 AS avg_ms
FROM dd.logs(columns => ARRAY['@duration'],
             filter => 'service:my-service @duration:*',
             from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '15 minute', to_timestamp => NOW())
     AS ("@duration" VARCHAR)
```

## Function reference

Pulled from <https://docs.datadoghq.com/ddsql_reference/>. Function support
varies by data source; if a call fails with "unsupported function", try a
plainer equivalent (e.g. `LIKE` instead of `REGEXP_LIKE`) or split the
expression across a CTE.

**Aggregates:** `COUNT`, `COUNT(DISTINCT …)`, `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT`,
`SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `BOOL_AND`, `BOOL_OR`,
`APPROX_PERCENTILE(p) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY expr)`. The
`COUNT(...) FILTER (WHERE ...)` form is **not** supported — use
`COUNT(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 END)` or a subquery instead.

**Strings:** `LENGTH`, `LOWER`, `UPPER`, `TRIM`, `REPLACE`, `SUBSTRING`,
`REVERSE`, `STRPOS`, `SPLIT_PART`, `||` (concat), `LIKE`.

**Numeric:** `ABS`, `CEIL` / `CEILING`, `FLOOR`, `ROUND`, `POWER`.

**Date/time:** `NOW()`, `EXTRACT(unit FROM …)`, `TO_TIMESTAMP`, `TO_CHAR`,
`DATE_BIN`, `DATE_TRUNC(unit, ts)`.
- `EXTRACT` units: `day`, `dow`, `doy`, `epoch`, `hour`, `minute`,
  `second`, `week`, `month`, `quarter`, `year`, `timezone_hour`,
  `timezone_minute`.
- `DATE_TRUNC` units: `milliseconds`, `seconds`, `minutes`, `hours`,
  `days`, `weeks`, `months`, `quarters`, `years`.

**Regex (ICU flavor):** `REGEXP_LIKE`, `REGEXP_MATCH`, `REGEXP_REPLACE`.
Flags: `i` (case-insensitive), `n`/`m` (newline-sensitive), `g` (replace
all). Not all backends accept regex; fall back to `LIKE` if a regex call
errors.

**JSON:** `json_extract_path_text(json, path…)`,
`json_extract_path(json, path…)`, `json_array_elements`,
`json_array_elements_text`. The `->` operator is **HSTORE-only** (tag
maps); for `JSON` columns always use `json_extract_path_text` then cast.
`->>` is unsupported on either type.

**Arrays:** `ARRAY[a, b, c]`, `CARDINALITY`, `ARRAY_POSITION`,
`STRING_TO_ARRAY`, `ARRAY_TO_STRING`, `ARRAY_AGG`, `UNNEST`. **`UNNEST`
must be used as a table reference in `FROM`** (`SELECT x FROM UNNEST(arr)
AS x`), not in the `SELECT` list. It also cannot appear directly in
`GROUP BY` — wrap in a subquery or CTE (see Examples). Array subscript
syntax (`a[1]`) is unsupported; use `ARRAY_POSITION` or `UNNEST` instead.

**Window functions:** `OVER (PARTITION BY … ORDER BY …)`, `RANK`,
`ROW_NUMBER`, `LEAD`, `LAG`, `FIRST_VALUE`, `LAST_VALUE`, `NTH_VALUE`.

**INET:** `host`, `network`, `netmask`, `masklen`, `broadcast`, `family`.
Operators `<<`, `<<=`, `>>`, `>>=`, `&&` for containment / overlap.

**Utility:** `COALESCE`, `CAST(value AS type)`. Castable targets:
`BIGINT`, `DECIMAL`, `INET`, `TIMESTAMP`, `VARCHAR`.

## Table functions

Event-platform sources (logs, spans, RUM, events) are queried through
**polymorphic** PTFs: choose the columns to project in `columns =>
ARRAY[...]` and declare the output schema with `AS (col TYPE, ...)`.
Metric and cloud-cost PTFs are **monomorphic** — they have a fixed
output shape, so do **not** add `AS (...)`.

```sql
-- Logs (polymorphic). dd.spans, dd.rum, dd.events take the same shape.
SELECT service, status
FROM dd.logs(
  columns => ARRAY['service', 'status'],
  filter => 'service:my-service',          -- Datadog log search syntax
  from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour',
  to_timestamp => NOW()
) AS (service VARCHAR, status VARCHAR)
ORDER BY service
LIMIT 20

-- Metrics (monomorphic). Returns columns: tags, value.
SELECT tags, value
FROM dd.metrics_scalar('avg:system.cpu.user{*} by {host}', 'avg')
ORDER BY value DESC
LIMIT 20

-- Metrics timeseries (monomorphic). Returns: timestamp, tags, value.
SELECT timestamp, tags, value
FROM dd.metrics_timeseries('avg:system.cpu.user{host:my-host}')
ORDER BY timestamp

-- Cloud Cost (monomorphic, same shape as metrics).
SELECT tags, value
FROM dd.cloud_cost_scalar('sum:aws.cost.amortized{*} by {service}', 'sum')
LIMIT 20
```

`dd.logs`, `dd.spans`, `dd.rum`, and `dd.events` all share the same
event-platform PTF signature. Optional arguments include
`indexes => ARRAY[...]` and `storage => 'hot' | 'flex_tier'`.

Notes:
- Nested fields use dot notation; non-core fields take an `@` prefix and
  must be quoted (`"@http.status_code"`).
- Inventory tables (`dd.hosts`, `dd.agent_hosts`, etc.) are **not** PTFs
  — use plain `FROM dd.hosts` (see "Tags" below).
- Cloud Cost data is delayed by 24–48 hours.
- The metrics PTF `query` argument is itself a metric query string in the
  standard Datadog format (e.g. `avg:system.cpu.user{host:foo}`), not a
  bare metric name.

## Tags

Inventory tables (`dd.hosts`, `dd.agent_hosts`, cloud resources, …) expose
`tags` as an HSTORE-style map. Access with the `->` operator:

```sql
SELECT hostname, tags->'env' AS env
FROM dd.hosts
WHERE tags->'team' = 'foo'
LIMIT 20
```

Inventory tables are queried with plain `FROM dd.<table>` — no PTF
wrapper, no time arguments. Discover columns with
`ddsql_schema_get_table_columns`.

Helpers: `AKEYS(tags)` (all keys), `AVALS(tags)` (all values). When a tag
key has multiple values, `tags->'k'` returns them comma-separated.

Event tables (logs, spans, RUM) instead expose tags as an array of
`key:value` strings. To group by a tag value there, project the tag array
in the PTF `columns` and `UNNEST` it (see Examples).

## `extra_columns`

When a tool exposes an `extra_columns` parameter for projecting additional
fields with declared types, only these type names are accepted:

```
varchar, bigint, decimal, boolean, timestamp, json,
array<varchar>, array<bigint>, array<decimal>, array<boolean>, array<timestamp>
```

Caveats:
- `json`-typed extra columns can only be referenced through
  `json_extract_path_text(...)`, then cast. They cannot be filtered,
  grouped, or compared directly.
- The legacy aliases `string` / `int64` / `float64` / `bool` and their
  `array<…>` variants are accepted but the canonical names above are
  preferred.

## Working examples

Each example uses the PTF form, which is required when executing through
`ddsql_run_query`. Treat them as templates: replace columns and filters
to match the dataset returned during schema discovery, and adjust the
time window in `from_timestamp` / `to_timestamp` for the question at
hand.

### Count by status

```sql

FROM dd.logs(
  columns => ARRAY['status'],
  filter => '*',
  from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour',
  to_timestamp => NOW()
) AS (status VARCHAR)
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY cnt DESC
LIMIT 10
```

### Top services by error count

```sql
SELECT service, COUNT(*) AS errors
FROM dd.logs(
  columns => ARRAY['service'],
  filter => 'status:error',

  to_timestamp => NOW()
) AS (service VARCHAR)
GROUP BY service
ORDER BY errors DESC
LIMIT 10
```

### Time bucketing (repeat the expression in `GROUP BY`)

```sql
SELECT
  DATE_TRUNC('minute', timestamp) AS bucket,
  COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM dd.logs(
  columns => ARRAY['timestamp'],
  filter => 'status:error',
  from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour',
  to_timestamp => NOW()
) AS (timestamp TIMESTAMP)
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('minute', timestamp)
ORDER BY bucket DESC
LIMIT 60
```

### Quoting an `@`-prefixed unstructured field

```sql
SELECT "@http.status_code", COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM dd.logs(
  columns => ARRAY['@http.status_code'],
  filter => '@http.status_code:*',
  from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour',
  to_timestamp => NOW()
) AS ("@http.status_code" VARCHAR)
GROUP BY "@http.status_code"
ORDER BY cnt DESC
LIMIT 10
```

### Casting an unstructured field for arithmetic

`@`-prefixed fields commonly arrive as arrays of strings even when they
look scalar. Cast inside the aggregate.

```sql
SELECT
  service,
  AVG(CAST("@duration" AS BIGINT)) / 1000000 AS avg_ms
FROM dd.logs(
  columns => ARRAY['service', '@duration'],
  filter => 'service:my-service @duration:* status:ok',
  from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '15 minute',
  to_timestamp => NOW()
) AS (service VARCHAR, "@duration" VARCHAR)
GROUP BY service
ORDER BY avg_ms DESC
LIMIT 10
```

### Conditional severity bucket (`CASE`)

`GROUP BY` repeats the full `CASE` expression; aliases are not allowed
there.

```sql
SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN status IN ('error','critical','emergency','alert') THEN 'severe'
    WHEN status IN ('warn','notice') THEN 'mid'
    ELSE 'low'
  END AS severity,
  COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM dd.logs(
  columns => ARRAY['status'],
  filter => '*',
  from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour',
  to_timestamp => NOW()
) AS (status VARCHAR)
GROUP BY
  CASE
    WHEN status IN ('error','critical','emergency','alert') THEN 'severe'
    WHEN status IN ('warn','notice') THEN 'mid'
    ELSE 'low'
  END
ORDER BY cnt DESC
```

### Conditional aggregate (replacement for `FILTER (WHERE …)`)

DDSQL doesn't support `COUNT(...) FILTER (WHERE ...)`. Use a
`CASE`-inside-aggregate instead.

```sql
SELECT
  service,
  COUNT(*) AS errors,
  COUNT(CASE WHEN "@http.status_code" IS NOT NULL THEN 1 END) AS http_errors
FROM dd.logs(
  columns => ARRAY['service', '@http.status_code'],
  filter => 'status:error',
  from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour',
  to_timestamp => NOW()
) AS (service VARCHAR, "@http.status_code" VARCHAR)
GROUP BY service
ORDER BY errors DESC
LIMIT 10
```

### Expanding an array column with `UNNEST`

`UNNEST` must appear in `FROM`, not in the `SELECT` list, and cannot be
referenced directly in `GROUP BY`. Put `UNNEST(arr) AS x` in `FROM` and
aggregate over `x`. This is the equivalent of Splunk's `mvexpand`.

This example pivots host IPs out of `dd.hosts.ip_addresses`
(`array_of_string`):

```sql
SELECT ip, COUNT(*) AS hosts
FROM dd.hosts, UNNEST(ip_addresses) AS ip
WHERE ip_addresses IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY ip
ORDER BY hosts DESC
LIMIT 10
```

For event tables (logs, spans, RUM), most projected fields come back as
scalars even when conceptually multi-valued — when you need to expand
one, project it from the PTF, then `UNNEST` in `FROM` of an outer CTE.

### `HAVING` to filter aggregate results

```sql
SELECT service, status, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM dd.logs(
  columns => ARRAY['service', 'status'],
  filter => 'status:(error OR warn OR critical)',
  from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour',
  to_timestamp => NOW()
) AS (service VARCHAR, status VARCHAR)
GROUP BY service, status
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1000
ORDER BY cnt DESC
LIMIT 20
```

### Paging through results (`OFFSET` before `LIMIT`)

```sql
SELECT service
FROM dd.logs(
  columns => ARRAY['service'],
  filter => '*',
  from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '15 minute',
  to_timestamp => NOW()
) AS (service VARCHAR)
ORDER BY service
OFFSET 20 LIMIT 20
```

## Joins

Supported join keywords: `JOIN`, `INNER JOIN`, `LEFT JOIN`, `RIGHT JOIN`,
`FULL JOIN`, `OUTER`, `ON`, `USING`. **`CROSS JOIN` is not supported** —
use the comma form `FROM a, b` for an explicit cross-product.

A few rules apply specifically to joins:

- **Each event PTF can only appear once per query.** Calling
  `dd.logs(...)` twice in the same `FROM` is rejected. For self-joins,
  project the PTF into a CTE once and join the CTE to itself.
- **Subtracting two `TIMESTAMP`s is rejected** with
  *"Cannot cast interval day to second to timestamp(3)"*. To get a
  duration in seconds, extract epoch from each side separately:
  `EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM b.ts) - EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM a.ts)`. Do **not** write
  `EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (b.ts - a.ts))`.
- **Quote camelCase columns in join keys.** Unquoted identifiers fold to
  lowercase, so `ON a.correlationId = b.correlationId` resolves as
  `correlationid` and fails to match. Use `ON a."correlationId" = b."correlationId"`.
- **Reference tables live under `reference_tables.<name>`** and must
  exist. Discover them with `ddsql_schema_search_tables` before joining
  — `JOIN some_table` against an unknown name returns *"depends on
  non-existent dataset"*.

### Pairing start/completed events with a self-join

Project the PTF into a CTE once, label each row with a phase, then join
the CTE to itself on a correlation key. Compute the duration via two
epoch extractions, never via timestamp subtraction.

```sql
WITH ev AS (
  SELECT trace_id, timestamp AS ts,
         CASE WHEN message LIKE '%Starting%' THEN 'started'
              WHEN message LIKE '%completed%' THEN 'completed' END AS phase
  FROM dd.logs(
    columns => ARRAY['trace_id', 'timestamp', 'message'],
    filter => 'service:my-service (Starting OR completed)',
    from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '15 minute',
    to_timestamp => NOW()
  ) AS (trace_id VARCHAR, timestamp TIMESTAMP, message VARCHAR)
  WHERE trace_id IS NOT NULL
),
paired AS (
  SELECT s.trace_id,
         EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM c.ts) - EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM s.ts) AS duration_s
  FROM ev s
  JOIN ev c ON s.trace_id = c.trace_id
  WHERE s.phase = 'started' AND c.phase = 'completed' AND c.ts > s.ts
)
SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS pairs,
  APPROX_PERCENTILE(0.50) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY duration_s) AS p50_s,
  APPROX_PERCENTILE(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY duration_s) AS p95_s,
  MAX(duration_s) AS max_s
FROM paired
```

### Joining an event source against an inventory table

Inventory tables (`dd.hosts`, `dd.agent_hosts`, …) plug into a join
with no PTF wrapper. Project the event side into a CTE first, then join
in the outer query.

```sql
WITH errs AS (
  SELECT host, COUNT(*) AS cnt
  FROM dd.logs(
    columns => ARRAY['host'],
    filter => 'status:error',
    from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '15 minute',
    to_timestamp => NOW()
  ) AS (host VARCHAR)
  GROUP BY host
)
SELECT h.hostname, h.tags->'env' AS env, e.cnt
FROM errs e
JOIN dd.hosts h ON h.hostname = e.host
ORDER BY e.cnt DESC
LIMIT 20
```

### Joining a reference table

Replace `service_catalog_teams` with whatever reference table you found
via `ddsql_schema_search_tables`.

```sql
WITH errs AS (
  SELECT service, COUNT(*) AS cnt
  FROM dd.logs(
    columns => ARRAY['service'],
    filter => 'status:error',
    from_timestamp => NOW() - INTERVAL '15 minute',
    to_timestamp => NOW()
  ) AS (service VARCHAR)
  GROUP BY service
)
SELECT t.team, e.service, e.cnt
FROM errs e
JOIN reference_tables.service_catalog_teams t ON t.service = e.service
ORDER BY e.cnt DESC
LIMIT 20
```

## Common pitfalls

| Wrong | Right |
|---|---|
| `FROM logs` via `ddsql_run_query` | `FROM dd.logs(columns => ARRAY[...], from_timestamp => ..., to_timestamp => ...) AS (col TYPE, ...)` |
| `GROUP BY bucket` (alias) | `GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('hour', timestamp)` |
| `WHERE @level = 'error'` | `WHERE "@level" = 'error'` |
| `WHERE timestamp > NOW() - INTERVAL '1 day'` on an event PTF | bound time via `from_timestamp` / `to_timestamp` PTF args instead |
| `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10` | `OFFSET 10 LIMIT 20` |
| `TIMESTAMP '2026-02-05Z'` or `'2026-02-05'` | `TIMESTAMP '2026-02-05 00:00:00+00:00'` |
| `AVG("@duration")` on an unstructured numeric | `AVG(CAST("@duration" AS BIGINT))` |
| `json_col ->> 'k'` or `json_col -> 'k'` | `json_extract_path_text(json_col, 'k')` (`->` is HSTORE-only) |
| `tags ->> 'env'` | `tags->'env'` |
| `SELECT UNNEST(arr) AS x ...` | `SELECT x FROM ... AS (..., arr ARRAY<...>), UNNEST(arr) AS x` |
| `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE cond)` | `COUNT(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 END)` |
| `arr[1]` | `ARRAY_POSITION(arr, value)` or `UNNEST(arr)` |
| `WHERE col = ANY(ARRAY[...])` | `WHERE col IN (...)` |
| `CROSS JOIN` | `FROM a, b` (comma cross-product) |
| `EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (b.ts - a.ts))` | `EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM b.ts) - EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM a.ts)` |
| `dd.logs(...) a JOIN dd.logs(...) b` | project once into CTE, then self-join the CTE |
| `JOIN logs ON a.correlationId = b.correlationId` | quote camelCase: `ON a."correlationId" = b."correlationId"` |
| `JOIN team_to_service` (bare reference table) | `JOIN reference_tables.team_to_service` |

## Source-specific guidance

Bundled resources cover individual data sources in depth (event-type
schemas, relationships, query recipes, domain-specific caveats):

- **RUM** (Real User Monitoring): `references/rum.md`. **The default query
  path for RUM data when this skill is loaded alongside `datadog/rum`.**
  Required reading before composing any `dd.rum(...)` query - `event_type`
  is a required PTF argument with a fixed set of valid values. Covers the
  seven PTF event types, session → view → child-event relationships, Core
  Web Vitals, common recipes, and the workaround paths for operations
  (currently not PTF-queryable).
